newsitem.title: UK: Ecuador crisis may not be so awful for investors.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador crisis may not be so awful for investors.

text.p: The political chaos in Ecuador is not a complete disaster for investors even though they have had to watch the country's debt price tumble along with the political fortunes of ousted President Abdala Bucaram, analysts said on Friday.
Ecuador's Brady bonds -- rescheduled debt turned into interest-bearing bonds -- have slumped almost 14 percent in two weeks, the worst performer in the emerging debt market.

The main pressure on the price has been the plight of Bucaram who on Thursday was suddenly ousted by Congress on Thursday but has refused to quit and make way for their appointee congressional leader Fabian Alarcon.

"The underlying economic situation in Ecuador is far from disastrous," said West Merchant Bank economic adviser Peter West, pointing to a positive balance of payments and relative control over inflation.
Few expect Bucaram, his credibility in shreds, to be able to hang on to power, with elections likely over the next year.
The populist Bucaram had managed, initially, to convince most investors that he was serious about economic reform but analysts said it was his personality which appears to have been his undoing.

"There is still hope they can do reforms if the personalities are right," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's head of emerging market research Paul Luke, adding that Ecuador Brady prices were now very close to buy levels.

He noted one sign was that the spread differential between Ecuador and Brazil par bonds had widened to almost exactly the same level the last time investors panicked over Ecuador. That was when it became clear Bucaram was going to become president.
Few expected his loss of power would be so rapid, though Ecuador's Congress has a long record of being trigger happy with impeachments of senior officials.
ABN-AMRO analyst Ian Campbell said there was still a danger that even if a more investor-friendly president eventually came to power, that the problems of Ecuador's political system would continue.
He was concerned the fiscal side of the economy, noting that Bucaram had reversed necessary tarrif increases.
He also doubted that plans to introduce a currency board would now be implemented, which many analysts said anyway had not been such a great idea.
However, while the short-term wis bound to offer investors a bumpy ride, over the longer time the outlook is reasonable.
"In six months, we will have better economic management with out Bucaram than with him," said ANZ analyst Jerome Booth.
There could well be some slippage on reform but there was unlikely to be serious backtracking, he added.
